title: Hotpath release sentinels and backstops
content:
Purpose:
This is my personal scratchpad for a hotpath-focused canary plan and the escape/backstop tactics I want in place before any release that touches low-latency request paths (chat streaming, short-response generator endpoints). Not a polished runbook — thinking out loud + TODOs + quick checks.

Background/context:
- Hotpath endpoints are our 95th-99th tail sensitivity areas: small increases in queueing or kernel stalls quickly become customer-facing error spikes.
- Recent infra changes (memory allocator tweak + batcher heuristic) interacted badly with a particular model variant in 2025-09 and produced a 3x P95 latency for 15 minutes. Need stronger preflight and real-time sentinels for these releases.

High-level strategy (conceptual):
1) Preflight: synthetic microbench + short-duration soak, run against realistic token distributions (short prompts, streaming enabled).
2) Canary: phased traffic windows with explicit hotpath cohorts (10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100%) but separate the hotpath cohort from background embedding/large-batch traffic.
3) Sentinels: real-time telemetry slices that can trigger partial or full automatic rollback or traffic diversion.
4) Backstops: network-level and API-level escape hatches that are fast to execute (feature flag + route-level pin + emergency model downgrade).

Preflight checklist (short):
- [ ] Run microbench harness for 1/3/10/30s piles with 90/95/99 token sequences, collect P50/P95/P99 and allocations.
- [ ] Compare local kernel selection trace vs canary image to ensure identical kernels selected (avoid silent perf drift).
- [ ] Run streaming test with 50 concurrent connections for 60s (verify fragment streaming response times).
- [ ] Verify kv-cache warm-up under the canary image and ensure cache-hit rates >= baseline - 5%.
- [ ] Validate GPU memory fragmentation profile; ensure no allocation failure events in allocator logs.
- [ ] Smoke test fallback path: force fallback to quantized variant and confirm correctness and connection stability.

Canary rollout plan (numeric windows):
- Window A (5 minutes): 1% traffic to hotpath cohort; monitor for error rate and tail latency.
- Window B (15 minutes): 5% traffic; still restrict to internal customers + opt-in beta users.
- Window C (30 minutes): 20% traffic; broader beta + external small pools.
- Window D (60 minutes): 50% traffic; monitor for sustained trends.
- Final (ramp to 100%): only if windows show stable metrics for 2x window durations.
Notes: separate schedule for other routes — avoid mixing heavy batch embedding jobs with hotpath canary.

Sentinels (signals and thresholds):
- Latency:
  - P95 increase > 30% relative to baseline for 5m window -> alert (page on-call SRE).
  - P99 increase > 20% relative to baseline for 2m window -> immediate traffic hold for canary cohort.
  - Streaming-first-byte (SFB) increase > 25% for 3m -> alert.
- Errors:
  - 5xx rate > 0.2% absolute or > 3x baseline -> immediate hold + runbook check.
  - gRPC status RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED occurrences > 1 per minute -> emergency backout.
- Resource telemetry:
  - GPU SM utilization drop > 25% with concurrent increase in queue length -> probe batcher/kernels.
  - CUDA OOM or allocator fail events -> immediate rollback.
- User-facing heuristics:
  - Session-level tail tokens truncated > 0.5% of sessions -> keep canary on hold and investigate.

Automated responses (fast actions):
- Soft hold: set canary traffic to 0% via release controller (automated, <10s to apply). Log gating reason and notify Slack #releases.
- Partial diversion: move hotpath cohort requests to cached-responses path for 30 minutes (if cache matches tolerance) while SRE inspects.
- Model downgrade: replace model variant with nearest-compatible quantized variant (pre-warmed image) for the cohort. This should be scriptable with a single CLI and take <60s.
- Full rollback: revert canary image to previous pinned version and set rollout to blocked until manual review.

Manual response playbook (on-call steps):
1) Confirm signal: check metrics window + raw traces (APM).
2) Check kernel selection logs for the canary pod(s) implicated.
3) If P99 spike and allocation events present -> downgrade model variant immediately.
4) If error rate spike without alloc events -> increase logging and enable detailed request sampling for 1 minute.
5) If unknown cause after 10m -> full rollback and incident declared.

Pinning and variant strategy notes (how I want to manage versions):
- Always keep a named "hotpath-stable" pin for each route that maps to a tested model image. Changes to hotpath-stable must go through this canary flow.
- Keep pre-baked downgrade variants: e.g., model-x:quant-fp16 and model-x:int8. They must be kept warm on dedicated pool for <2s failover.
- Use semantic channel tags: release candidates labeled rc/<date>-<sha> and a separate stable tag. Release controller operates on tags, not raw SHAs when possible.

Edge-case mitigations (unique ideas to test):
- Token-budget enforcement: for short-response hotpaths, enforce per-request token budget soft limits in the canary to ensure one heavy attacker request doesn’t back up the pool.
- Early tail-trimming: if a request hits 2x median generation time, serve last-known-good partial and mark the session degraded (avoid full 500s).
- Backpressure-to-client: if internal queue length > threshold, return 429 with Retry-After to a small fraction of non-critical clients to protect latency for premium cohorts.

Quick checklist before enabling auto-responses: 
- [ ] Confirm Slack webhook and Opsgenie runbook links are valid.
- [ ] Smoke the downgrade script end-to-end from staging (no human intervention).
- [ ] Verify traffic hold API responds within 10s under high load.
- [ ] Add temporary extra sampling (10%) for request traces for the first two windows.

Notes-to-self / open questions:
- Is the pre-warmed downgrade pool costly? Need to estimate: two extra model variants warming consumes ~1.5x baseline GPU capacity for small fleets. Ask infra for cost estimate.
- Consider flag for ephemeral cache-only mode (no compute) so we can divert low-cost traffic when GPUs are flapping. Who owns the cache route? Tagging Priya.
- Should we gate canary by region to reduce blast radius (use EU region for EU-only initial windows)? Probably yes; add into rollout controller config.

Action items (short):
- [Jamie] Wireup simple CLI that executes: set-pin, quick-downgrade, set-canary-traffic. (blockers: auth scopes).
- [Anita] Calculate cost delta for keeping two pre-warmed downgrade variants.
- [Derek] Add P99 kernel-selection telemetry to the canary dashboard and a quick-link for kernel diffs.
- [Priya] Confirm cache diversion endpoint exists and document its semver compatibility constraints.

Final thought: prioritize small, fast, reversible levers rather than complex reactive logic. For hotpath routes the ability to flip a single flag or swap to a pre-warmed variant within a minute buys a lot of safety. This doc is my working crib notes for the next release; will formalize into the release playbook if any of these get used for a real incident.

-- jm
